meta.tagline: Dock scheduling and driver messaging for mid-size freight forwarders

slides.title: Meridian
slides.subtitle: Dock scheduling and driver messaging for mid-size freight forwarders
slides.question: What is this, in plain words?
slides.notes:
Say: Meridian is dock scheduling and driver messaging for mid-size freight forwarders. 32 customers pay us EUR 41,200 a month, an ARR run-rate of EUR 494,400.
Context: MRR is recurring subscription revenue from live customers in October 2026. A contract that is signed but not live is not counted.
Transition: Here is what a dock looks like without us.
Time: 30

slides.title: One Hamburg site paid *EUR 38,000* in truck waiting fees in 2024

points.text: Three dispatchers, six phones, a paper notebook and a WhatsApp group of about 60 drivers
60 percent of trucks arrive between 06:00 and 09:30; the docks stand idle in the afternoon
Carriers used to absorb the waiting time. Now they invoice it after 90 minutes

stats.label: waiting fees paid at one site in 2024
average dock wait per truck at that site, March to May 2024

slides.question: Who hurts, how much, and what do they do about it now?
slides.notes:
Say: This is one of our customers before Meridian: a forwarder with three sites and about 400 truck movements a day. The mess has a price tag now, because carriers invoice the wait.
Context: These figures are one site in one year, from the customer's own records. We do not yet have fee totals across customers.
Transition: So we started with the driver, not the dispatcher.
Time: 75

slides.title: Carriers book by link, and dock wait fell from 94 to *65 minutes* at one site

before.label: Before: phone and WhatsApp
before.text: Average dock wait per truck, March to May 2024

after.label: After: Meridian
after.text: Same site, March to May 2025, the first three months live

points.text: The booking link goes out with the transport order. No app, no login
Drivers get SMS or WhatsApp updates in German, English, Polish or Romanian
Dispatchers work from one inbox instead of six phones

slides.question: What do you do about it, and for whom?
slides.notes:
Say: A carrier gets a link with the transport order and books a dock slot. No app, no account. At the first site that cut dock wait by 31 percent.
Context: One customer, one site, three months in 2025, measured from the customer's gate logs against the same months a year earlier. It is not a company-wide figure.
Transition: This is how a truck moves through the product.
Time: 75

slides.title: Every truck knows where to go and when, *without a phone call*

points.text: Live with paying customers since January 2025
The first site went live in 11 working days
Reports: wait per carrier, dock use, no-show rate

slides.question: Does it exist, and does it do what you say?
slides.notes:
Say: Four parts: slot booking, driver messages, a yard board for the gatehouse and reports. All four are live today at 32 customers.
Context: Product screenshots are not in this version of the deck. Not built yet: TMS integrations, planned for Q2 2027; three of six interviewed customers asked for an integration we do not have.
Transition: Does it sell? Here are 22 months of revenue.
Time: 60

slides.title: Proof: customers *pay and stay*
slides.subtitle: Twenty-two months of revenue, three customers lost, one measured site

slides.title: MRR grew *2.15x* in twelve months to EUR 41,200
slides.question: Is this working, and how fast?
slides.notes:
Say: MRR went from EUR 19,200 to EUR 41,200 in twelve months, from EUR 4,100 in January 2025. We add 1.5 customers a month and have lost 3 in 22 months.
Context: In percentage terms growth is slowing: the line is straight because two founders do the selling. We have not measured net revenue retention or CAC payback yet.
Transition: This is what one head of operations says about it.
Time: 120

slides.quote: I do not need a yard management system. I need the drivers to *stop calling me*. That is what happened.
slides.role: Hamburg freight forwarder, 3 sites, about 400 truck movements a day

stat.label: fewer dock wait minutes at the main site, March to May 2025 against 2024

slides.question: Does a real customer get the value you claim?
slides.notes:
Say: This is the sentence we hear in every first call: stop the phone calls. At this site the wait went from 94 to 65 minutes per truck.
Context: One site, three months, 2025. The quote is from the published case study.
Transition: Why does it work? Because of who we built it for.
Time: 30

slides.title: Everyone builds for the dispatcher. We build for *the driver*.

nodes.title: Driver books by link
nodes.text: Built for 20 seconds in the cab

slides.question: Why does this work now, and why will you be the one to build it?
slides.notes:
Say: If a subcontractor driver can use it in 20 seconds, the dispatcher's life gets better automatically. Messaging is the wedge, the schedule is the lock-in.
Context: 20 seconds is our design target, not a measurement. Three customers lost in 22 months is the evidence we have for the lock-in so far.
Transition: Now the business.
Time: 75

slides.title: Mid-market is *the segment*, not a stepping stone
slides.subtitle: The business: market, pricing, how we sell and who else is there

slides.title: We estimate *EUR 216M* a year in DACH and Benelux alone

stats.label: TAM: the Europe-wide company count is not sourced yet
SAM: 14,000 companies in DACH and Benelux x EUR 1,288 a month x 12 (assumption)
Today: ARR run-rate from 32 paying customers, October 2026 (fact)

points: Company count: our desk research on Destatis and Eurostat, companies with 2 or more sites, 2025
Revenue per customer is our October 2026 average across 32 customers
slides.question: How big can this get, and how do you know?
slides.notes:
Say: We count about 14,000 companies in our size band in DACH and Benelux. At what customers pay us today that is about EUR 216M a year.
Context: The 14,000 is an estimate from 2025 desk research; the Europe-wide count is not done. The lower size limit of the band is still open between 50 and 150 truck movements a day.
Transition: Here is what one customer pays.
Time: 60

slides.title: A customer pays *EUR 1,288* a month on average, priced per site

stats.label: gross margin, a model input, not yet from the accounts (assumption)

points.text: A monthly subscription per site, paid by the operator
Per-site pricing undercharges our biggest customers; per-movement pricing is planned for Q4 2027

slides.question: Who pays, how much, and does a euro in produce more than a euro out?
slides.notes:
Say: One model: a subscription per site per month. Customers run one to several sites, so the average customer pays EUR 1,288 a month.
Context: We have not measured net revenue retention or CAC payback. Gross margin is the model's input. We burn EUR 53,800 a month net.
Transition: How do we find the next customers?
Time: 75

slides.title: Two founders close *1.5 customers a month*. The round pays for a sales team.

stats.label: new customers a month, average over 22 months
annual contract value of 18 open deals, unweighted

points: Beachhead: forwarders, 3PLs and cross-dock operators with 2 to 15 sites in DACH and Benelux
All 18 open deals are owned by a founder; no deal has yet closed without one
slides.question: How do you get customers repeatably, and what does one cost?
slides.notes:
Say: Every customer so far came from our network, two trade shows and referrals. We have not spent on paid marketing. The model assumes 4 new customers a month in 2027.
Context: 4 a month rests on account executives closing without a founder, which has not happened yet. We have no sales cycle data in a file.
Transition: Who else do prospects look at?
Time: 75

slides.title: “Everything in this industry is built for DHL. *We are not DHL.*”
slides.subtitle: COO of a five-site freight forwarder, after turning down an enterprise yard system, June 2025
slides.notes:
Say: This is a customer explaining why she turned down an enterprise yard system and bought from us.
Context: From our interview notes of June 2025; she became a customer in September 2025.
Transition: So this is how the alternatives compare.
Time: 20

slides.title: Enterprise systems serve the large shipper. Meridian serves *the forwarder*.
rows: 11 working days at the first site
points: From our notes on prospects and trade shows, July 2026; not checked against public pages
slides.question: Why will you win against the obvious alternatives, and why won't the incumbent copy you?
slides.notes:
Say: Most of our market still runs on a whiteboard, a phone and WhatsApp. The enterprise systems are ahead of us on integrations, and we say so.
Context: If an enterprise vendor shipped a light mid-market product, it would hurt. Our lead is the driver side and the speed of rollout.
Transition: Who is building this?
Time: 60

slides.title: Lena ran operations at an 11-site forwarder. Jonas built *carrier messaging*.

team.name: Lena Ostrowski
team.bio: 9 years in logistics operations. Head of Operations DACH at a mid-size forwarder with 11 sites and about 900 people: the job our customers have.

team.name: Jonas Hebbel
team.bio: 11 years in software. Led a fleet routing team of about 20 engineers; before that, SMS and WhatsApp messaging at a telco provider. Built version one alone in 5 months.

points: Lena was a customer of Jonas's previous company. Team of 7 in Berlin, with a former dispatcher in customer success
slides.question: Why these people, and who writes the code?
slides.notes:
Say: Lena spent four years buying yard management systems that never got rolled out. Jonas built the first version alone in 5 months while Lena sold it to the first 3 customers.
Context: Lena still does most demos herself. One account executive joined in April 2026.
Transition: That is what the round is for.
Time: 60

slides.question: How much, for what, and what will be true when it is spent?
slides.notes:
Say: EUR 3M, one priced round. 60 percent goes into go-to-market. Today we hold EUR 380,000, which is 7.1 months at the current burn.
Context: The model is being revised. On its own losses the round lasts 18.9 months, to mid 2028; the ARR at that point is the number still missing from this slide.
